Forensic Science & Violence

Forensic science basics — medico-legal cases, types of injuries, violence and the nurse’s role in evidence and victim care.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Define forensic science and its branches
  • Describe types of injuries and their medico-legal importance
  • Identify victims of violence
  • Explain the nurse’s role in forensic cases

In simple words

Forensic science applies medical knowledge to legal problems. Forensic nursing cares for the victim and the evidence together — without destroying what the court will need.

Branches of forensic science

  • Forensic pathology and toxicology
  • Forensic medicine (clinical)
  • Criminalistics — fingerprints, ballistics, DNA
  • Forensic odontology and anthropology
  • Forensic psychology and psychiatry

Medico-legal cases

  • Unnatural death (accident, suicide, homicide)
  • Assault and physical violence
  • Sexual offences and abuse
  • poisoning
  • Burns and suspicious injuries
  • Custodial deaths, torture and police cases
  • Death during or after procedures

Types of injuries

Injury Features
Abrasion Superficial scrape of skin
Bruises (contusion) Blunt force, blood under skin; colour changes
Laceration Tear of skin with ragged edges
Incised wound Clean cut, longer than deep
Stab wound Deep, narrow puncture
Firearm injury Entry and exit wounds
Burns Scalds, flame, electrical, chemical
Fractures Bone injury with or without displacement

Violence

  • Domestic violence, child abuse, elder abuse
  • Sexual violence and trafficking
  • Occupational and mob violence
  • Nurse’s role: identify, care, protect, document, refer to counselling and legal aid

🔴 Care first, evidence second

Treat life-threatening problems first. Then, before cleaning, dressing or removing clothes, preserve evidence. Patient care and evidence collection must both be documented with time and signature.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Forensic science applies medical knowledge for legal purposes.
  2. Medico-legal cases include unnatural death, assault, abuse and poisoning.
  3. Injuries: abrasion, bruise, laceration, incised and stab wounds.
  4. Preserve clothing, stains, hair, blood and weapons without cleaning.
  5. Record every observation with time and date, and never alter records.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Entry and exit wounds differ in firearm injury.
  2. Burns may be accidental, suicidal or homicidal.
  3. Child abuse and sexual violence need mandatory reporting.
  4. Custodial death and torture complaints need immediate documentation.
  5. The nurse gives comfort and connects victims to legal and psychological help.

📌 Memory trick

Nursing order: C-E-D — Care, Evidence, Documentation.

60-second revision

  • Forensic science branches: pathology, toxicology, criminalistics, odontology.
  • Medico-legal cases: unnatural death, assault, abuse, poisoning, burns.
  • Types of injuries: abrasion, bruise, laceration, incised, stab, firearm.
  • Preserve evidence before cleaning and dressing.
  • Document time, findings, signature; never alter.

Test yourself

A superficial scrape of the skin is called:

Answer: B. An abrasion is a superficial scrape on the skin surface caused by friction.

Which is a medico-legal case?

Answer: B. Unnatural death from accident, suicide or homicide is a medico-legal case.

Before dressing a wound in a crime case, the nurse should:

Answer: B. Evidence on skin, clothing and wounds must be preserved and documented before cleaning or dressing.

A deep, narrow puncture wound is called a:

Answer: A. A stab wound is a deep, narrow puncture made by a pointed instrument.

Documentation of a forensic case should be:

Answer: B. Forensic documentation is timed, factual, complete and signed; records are never altered or destroyed.
